headlines.article_text: GM will switch to Nasdaq from the NYSE on Nov. 17 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points General Motors plans to transfer its common-stock listing from the New York Stock Exchange to Nasdaq, with trading expected to begin Nov. 17. The automaker expects to keep its “GM” ticker symbol, and the company says shareholders do not need to take action because of the transfer. The transfer would make GM eligible for potential inclusion in the Nasdaq-100 Index, while aligning the listing with GM’s technology-driven strategy. In this article GM NDAQ Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT General Motors Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Paul Jacobson addresses investors at the GM Tech Center in Warren, Michigan, Oct. 6, 2021. Courtesy GM DETROIT — General Motors plans to transfer shares of its common stock from the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq as the automaker attempts to position itself more as a technology-focused company. The Detroit automaker said Tuesday that it expects to begin trading as a Nasdaq -listed company on Nov. 17. Its ticker symbol is expected to remain "GM," the company said. "GM's customer-focused, technology-driven strategy is creating value for our stockholders, making Nasdaq a natural home for our listing as we grow," GM CFO Paul Jacobson said in a release. "We're grateful for our long-standing partnership with the New York Stock Exchange and its remarkable legacy." GM noted the move will provide eligibility for potential inclusion in the Nasdaq-100 Index . Current shareholders do not need to take any action with respect to the transfer, the company said. The switch marks a notable loss for the NYSE, as GM first listed on the exchange in 1911. The Detroit automaker also relisted on the stock exchange in 2010 following a government-backed bankruptcy. General Motors vs. Ford Motor stock GM follows other companies such as Walmart , DoorDash and Palantir Technologies that have transferred from the more traditional NYSE to the historically technology focused Nasdaq in recent years. Hilton Worldwide Holdings last week also announced plans to move trading from the NYSE to Nasdaq. The key drivers for a listing transfer differ from company to company, but the Nasdaq in 2024 said common reasons include "index inclusion opportunities, cost effective fee structure, brand visibility partnership, access to Nasdaq's event space, and Nasdaq's suite of investor relations and ESG products." GM's decision comes a week after the automaker held a technology-focused event where executives laid out the company's roadmap for artificial intelligence and self-driving vehicle technologies. Shares of GM, which has been aggressively buying back stock , have more than doubled since 2024. GM's stock closed Monday at $76.31 per share. The company's market cap is roughly $64.4 billion. headlines.article_text: HSBC shares slump on revenue miss, lender announces share buyback Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points HSBC's revenue rose year-on-year to $18.6 billion. The bank's third-quarter profit before tax rose 32% from a year earlier to $9.6 billion. In this article HSBC Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Dado Ruvic | Reuters Europe's largest bank HSBC on Tuesday announced a share buyback of up to $1 billion and reported third-quarter pretax profit that largely met analysts' estimates. Revenue at HSBC rose to $18.6 billion from $17.8 billion in the same period last year, while banking net interest income rose 6%, alongside the bank clocking higher fee income form its corporate and institutional banking and wealth business. HSBC's London-listed shares dropped 6.5% in early European deals Monday, putting them on course for the worst session since Apr. 3 2025. Earlier, shares in Hong Kong dropped 2.95% following the earnings release, which saw the bank approve a third interim dividend of 10 cents per share. Citi analysts cited a "mixed set of results," noting a 2% miss on revenue expectations but an 18.8% return on tangible equity in the year to date — significantly ahead of its medium-term guidance of around 17%. Here are HSBC's third-quarter results compared with the consensus estimates compiled by the bank. Pre-tax profit: $9.63 billion vs. $9.69 billion expected Revenue: $18.6 billion vs. $18.93 billion expected The bank's third-quarter profit before tax increased 32% from a year earlier to $9.6 billion, also reflecting the absence of $1.4 billion in legal provisions recorded in the same period last year. Higher revenue and lower credit losses also supported earnings. The bank's net interest income rose to $9.3 billion in the third quarter, supported by deposit growth and reinvestment of its "structural hedge at higher yields." Meanwhile, operating expenses decreased 12% year on year to $8.8 billion, largely due to non-recurrence of legal provisions recorded a year earlier. Excluding notable items, expenses rose amid inflation and higher spending on technology. Looking ahead, HSBC maintained its forecast for banking net interest income of at least $46 billion in 2026, while reiterating its target for return on average tangible equity — a metric for assessing profitability — of 17% or higher for 2026 through 2028, excluding notable items. The bank also expects revenue to grow annually through 2028, targeting 5% growth that year compared with 2027, excluding notable items and on a constant currency basis. HSBC said it remains on track to deliver operating expense growth of approximately 1% in 2026 on a target basis, although strong business performance could lead to additional performance-related pay and modestly higher cost growth. The bank said it had bought back $1 billion in shares announced at its interim results, and expects to complete another $1 billion in buybacks before its full-year 2026 results. headlines.title: The 'stablecoin sandwich': Why speeding up payments isn't so simple, according to Mastercard
headlines.summary: Stablecoins could enable faster payments, but slow conversions in supporting infrastructure could limit benefits, according to Mastercard executive.
headlines.article_text: Speeding up payments isn't so simple, according to Mastercard Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Stablecoins could be attractive for certain remittance corridors and less commonly traded currency pairs, Mastercard's Matthew Driver said. Faster stablecoin payments depend on infrastructure supporting conversions between fiat currencies and stablecoins, Driver added. Mastercard completed BVNK acquisition in August and launched new stablecoin payment and security solutions last week. In this article MA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT CHONGQING, CHINA - JULY 29: In this photo illustration, a person holds a smartphone displaying the logo of Mastercard Inc. (NYSE: MA), a global payments and technology company, with the company's distinctive red and yellow overlapping circles visible in the background, on July 29, 2025 in Chongqing, China. (Photo illustration by Cheng Xin/Getty Images) Cheng Xin | Getty Images News | Getty Images Stablecoins could offer faster and more efficient payments, but realizing their full potential requires further development of the infrastructure supporting them, according to Mastercard. Stablecoins, a type of cryptocurrency designed to keep a steady value via a peg to an asset like the U.S. dollar, could be attractive for certain remittance corridors and less commonly traded currency pairs, Matthew Driver, executive vice president of services for Asia Pacific at Mastercard, told CNBC in an interview. "You don't want to have a 'stablecoin sandwich,'" Driver said, referring to a slow on-ramp into stablecoins, a fast transaction in the middle and a slow off-ramp back into fiat currency. That won't necessarily translate into faster payments, he said. Connecting real-time payment systems to stablecoin exchanges on both ends of a transaction could help speed up payments, but "you still need to enable the infrastructure," he said, adding that market participants need to be able to use the technology effectively. Opportunities for stablecoin adoption could vary across markets. In Singapore, where retail payments are already highly efficient, stablecoins may have fewer applications in consumer transactions, while corporate payments could offer greater opportunities, Driver said. He also pointed to smart contracts as a potential use case for corporate payments, allowing transactions to be executed when certain conditions are met. Interest in stablecoins has increased following the establishment of the U.S. GENIUS Act, Driver said. His comments come as Mastercard expands its involvement in digital assets, including through its acquisition of stablecoin infrastructure provider BVNK, which was completed in August. Earlier this month, Mastercard and BVNK launched Global Money Platform, designed to help banks, fintechs and businesses manage payments involving traditional currencies and stablecoins through a single application programming interface. Beyond payment speed, Mastercard is also looking to incorporate blockchain and identity data to establish the same level of trust expected across other payment systems, Driver said.
